title: How does a soft fork switch on?
dek: A bit in a block can signal readiness. New rules take effect only after a deployment has counted enough signals, waited, and reached activation.

blocks.text: A miner sets a bit in a block header. That block still follows the old rules. So does the next one. A soft fork needs a separate agreement about when nodes will begin rejecting blocks that break the new rules.

BIP 9 supplies that agreement: count signals over a period, lock in the change if enough blocks signal, then wait another period before enforcing it. BIP 8 changes the clock and adds an option to require signalling at the deadline. In either case, signalling by miners does not measure how many users have upgraded their nodes.

figure.title: The block where the rules change
figure.caption: CSV and SegWit each passed through a counting period and a waiting period. Only the ACTIVE side enforces the new rules. The activation heights are recorded in BIP 9; the preceding periods are inferred from its rules.

blocks.text: Before BIP 9, a soft fork raised the block version number. Several upgrades could not run independently, a failed attempt used up a version, and the old mechanism allowed only a small number of upgrades. BIP 9’s authors wanted separate signals for separate deployments.

Reading the field as bits fixes all three. A signalling block must have 001 as its top three bits, which gives versions from 0x20000000 to 0x3FFFFFFF; a block whose top bits are anything else counts as signalling nothing. That leaves 29 bits for deployments, and two other top-bit patterns for future mechanisms.

blocks.title: One bit per deployment
blocks.caption: A hypothetical version that would signal for both recorded deployments at once: the top three bits must be 001, and the other 29 are free for deployments. csv used bit 0 and segwit bit 1.

blocks.text: Each deployment gets a bit and a window in which that bit counts. Setting it outside that window does not turn the rules on. A bit can eventually be reused, but the authors recommend a pause so old software does not mistake the next deployment for the previous one.

blocks.summary: Choosing and reusing a deployment bit

blocks.text: Each deployment names its bit, from 0 to 28, a starttime and a timeout. BIP 9 suggests a start about a month after a release that includes the change, and a timeout one year later. The timeout is what lets a bit be reused: in the authors’ words, a new use of a bit then clearly refers to a new BIP.

Reuse is allowed but not encouraged. A later deployment may take a bit once the previous one has timed out or activated, and BIP 9 recommends a pause in between. The authors give that fallow period two jobs: it helps detect buggy clients, and it leaves time for warnings and upgrades after a soft fork succeeds.

Every deployment is in one of five states: DEFINED, STARTED, LOCKED_IN, ACTIVE or FAILED. States change only at the boundaries of 2,016-block retarget periods, and every block in a period shares one. A block’s state never depends on its own version, only on its ancestors.

The clock is not the wall clock. BIP 9 compares starttime and timeout with the median time past of the block before each period begins, a value the chain itself makes monotonic. Once that reaches starttime, the deployment is STARTED and the bit means something.

At each boundary in STARTED, nodes count how many of the previous 2,016 blocks set the bit. At least 1,916 of them, 95 percent, moves the deployment to LOCKED_IN; on testnet the threshold was 1,512. If the timeout has been reached, the deployment fails instead, and that check comes first.

blocks.title: How close is enough?
blocks.caption: A single block can separate reaching the threshold from waiting another period. The thresholds belong to the specified deployment rules.

blocks.text: Once LOCKED_IN, the deployment waits exactly one period. No further tally can undo it. The next period is ACTIVE, and upgraded nodes enforce the new rules. Miners should keep signalling during the wait so uptake remains visible.

Explore the alternatives below: enough signals, one short, or a deadline reached first. BIP 9 checks the timeout before the count, so even a full period of signals cannot rescue an attempt whose timeout has arrived.

blocks.title: From signalling to rules
blocks.caption: A schematic run of periods. Choose a deployment, step through the boundaries, and set whether a counted period reaches the threshold. The counts are hypothetical.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: Signalling is not activation. A STARTED or LOCKED_IN deployment changes no rule; only ACTIVE blocks enforce it, at least one full period after the count that locked it in. (BIP 8’s MUST_SIGNAL period is the one exception: there, a block that fails to signal can itself be invalid.)

blocks.summary: Why the timeout wins, and how unknown upgrades are noticed

blocks.text: The order matters because bits are shared over time. If counting came first, the authors explain, two deployments on the same bit could collide: an old one locking in while a new one starts, both demanding that miners set the bit. Checking the timeout first rules that out.
Nodes that have not upgraded still notice. BIP 9 has software track unexpected bits as an unknown upgrade, and says it should warn loudly when one locks in.

The opening diagram uses CSV and SegWit, the deployments listed in BIP 9. Their recorded activation heights let us work backward to the waiting and counting periods. They do not tell us the exact count of signalling blocks; the diagram shows only the threshold that must have been met.

blocks.summary: Deployment dates, heights and source checks

blocks.text: BIP 9 keeps a small table of deployments. It records csv, the bundle of BIPs 68, 112 and 113, on bit 0 with a mainnet window from 1 May 2016 to 1 May 2017, and segwit on bit 1 from 15 November 2016 to 15 November 2017. The dates match the Unix times written in the deployment sections of BIP 68 and BIP 141, and this site’s build fails if they ever disagree.

The table records only where each deployment became active: block 419,328 for csv and 481,824 for segwit, both multiples of 2,016. The rules let us read backwards. csv must have been LOCKED_IN from block 417,312, which means blocks 415,296 to 417,311 included at least 1,916 that signalled; segwit was LOCKED_IN from 479,808.
Those dates are history, not a schedule. A deployment’s parameters describe one attempt at one time; the table’s states say how each attempt ended.

sections.heading: What happens if the deadline arrives?

blocks.text: BIP 8’s authors wanted to limit miners’ ability to delay a change and avoid a schedule tied to block timestamps. Their proposal uses block heights for the start and deadline. It also allows a minimum activation height, so a change can lock in without taking effect too soon.

The choice is lockinontimeout. Turn it off and an attempt without enough signals fails at the deadline. Turn it on and the final period becomes MUST_SIGNAL: once the permitted number of non-signalling blocks has been used, further non-signalling blocks are invalid. That forces the count needed for lock-in.

blocks.title: Two endings for a stalled deployment
blocks.caption: BIP 8’s suggested parameters, run by the tested model with no STARTED period reaching the threshold. Only lockinontimeout differs.

blocks.text: The choice can split nodes onto different chains. BIP 8 warns that nodes requiring lock-in may follow a lower-work chain than nodes that do not, potentially for an extended period. Its authors suggest this option for changes facing political opposition from a significant share of miners.

So a BIP 8 deployment counts in heights: startheight and timeoutheight, both on retarget boundaries and at least 4,032 blocks apart. Its suggested threshold is lower, 1,815 blocks or 90 percent, and its suggested window is probably at least a year, 52,416 blocks. A minimum activation height can hold a locked-in deployment back so that nodes have time to upgrade; set to 0, LOCKED_IN lasts one period, as in BIP 9.

The new part is lockinontimeout. Without it, a deployment that never reaches the threshold fails at the timeout. With it, the last period before the timeout becomes MUST_SIGNAL: once 2,016 minus the threshold blocks in it have failed to signal, any further block that fails to signal is invalid, and the deployment locks in regardless.

BIP 8’s own history is in its changelog: rejected after a three-year timeout in 2020, revised with MUST_SIGNAL and a minimum activation height, and advanced to complete in 2026. Its pinned assignments file lists no deployments.

blocks.summary: Proposal dates and status in the pinned sources

blocks.text: A soft fork tightens the rules in a backward-compatible way. Once it is active, blocks that older software would accept can be rejected, so everyone needs to know from which block the new rules apply. BIP 9, assigned in 2015 and recorded as deployed, is the mechanism that told them for the csv and segwit soft forks. BIP 8, assigned in 2017 and now recorded as complete, is an alternative that counts in block heights and can force the outcome.
